title: Perseus. Atlas. Andromeda
titleEn: The Wedding Feast, and the Battle with Phineus Begins — Metamorphoses IV.753–V.96
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Perseus, fresh from killing the sea-monster, builds three turf altars to Mercury, Minerva and Jupiter, and carries Andromeda off as the prize of the deed, without a dowry. At the wedding feast the Cephenes ask him how he took the Gorgon's head, and he tells them: the one eye the daughters of Phorcys shared, the road to the Gorgons' house past men and beasts turned to stone, the killing done by watching Medusa's reflection in his shield. Asked why Medusa alone wore snakes for hair, he answers that Neptune raped her in Minerva's temple and Minerva punished her by changing her hair. Book V opens without a break in the same hall: Phineus, Cepheus' brother and Andromeda's promised husband, bursts in to claim her, Cepheus answers him, and the wedding turns into a massacre in which Athis, Lycabas and a long file of named men are killed.

advisory.lede: This part contains the rape of Medusa by the sea-god Neptune in Minerva's temple, and the goddess's punishment of Medusa, not of the god, for it.
advisory.more: Perseus tells the story in four lines (IV.798-801), as an answer to a polite dinner-table question about why Medusa's hair was snakes. Neptune violated her in Minerva's temple; Minerva turned her face away, covered it with the aegis, and changed the raped woman's hair into snakes so that the offence should not go unpunished. The Latin verb is vitiasse, the blunt legal-sounding word for spoiling or ruining a woman, and the translation keeps its bluntness rather than softening it; the note on the unit says what the word is doing. The poem passes no judgement on the punishment falling entirely on the victim, and the text is presented unaltered.

sentences.t:
Dis tribus ille focos totidem de caespite ponit,
laevum Mercurio, dextrum tibi, bellica virgo,
ara Iovis media est.
sentences.l: To three gods he sets up as many hearth-altars of cut turf: the left one for Mercury, the right one for you, warlike maiden; the altar of Jupiter is the middle one.
sentences.i: For three gods he builds three altars of cut turf: the left for Mercury, the right for you, warrior maiden, and Jupiter's in the middle.
sentences.n: "tibi, bellica virgo" is apostrophe, the poet turning aside to speak to a character directly, here to Minerva; Ovid does it throughout the poem, and it is the first thing to watch for when an unexplained "you" appears. "totidem" means "just as many" and counts the altars against the gods. Turf altars cut from the ground are the improvised field altar of a traveller or soldier, made where no temple is.

sentences.t:
Mactatur vacca Minervae,
alipedi vitulus, taurus tibi, summe deorum.
sentences.l: A cow is slaughtered for Minerva, a calf for the wing-footed one, a bull for you, highest of the gods.
sentences.n: One verb ("mactatur") serves all three victims and the last two drop it entirely; the figure is zeugma and it makes the triple sacrifice one act. "alipedi" (wing-footed) names Mercury by an attribute rather than by name, the ordinary epic way of varying a god. The greatest of the three victims, the bull, is kept for Jupiter, and "tibi" is apostrophe again, now to him.

sentences.t:
protinus Andromedan et tanti praemia facti
indotata rapit:
sentences.l: At once he carries off Andromeda, the reward of so great a deed, undowered.
sentences.i: At once he carries Andromeda off as the prize of so great a deed, and takes her without a dowry.
sentences.n: "indotata" is neuter plural and agrees with "praemia", not with Andromeda: it is the prize that comes without a dowry, the rescue itself standing in for the settlement a bride's family would provide. "rapit" is the ordinary verb for carrying a bride off in a wedding, but it is also the verb for seizing by force, and Andromeda has already been carried off once, to the rock.

sentences.t:
taedas Hymenaeus Amorque
praecutiunt, largis satiantur odoribus ignes,
sentences.l: Hymenaeus and Love shake the torches out in front, the fires are sated with lavish perfumes,
sentences.i: Hymen and Love shake the wedding torches before them; the fires are glutted with heaped incense.
sentences.n: "praecutiunt" is prae- plus quatio, to brandish in front: the action of the torch-bearers who walk at the head of a bridal procession, here done by the gods themselves rather than by servants. Hymenaeus is the wedding-god grown out of the wedding-cry shouted at Roman weddings. "largis ... odoribus" is ablative with the passive "satiantur", the fires fed until they can take no more.

sentences.t:
sertaque dependent tectis et ubique lyraeque
tibiaque et cantus, animi felicia laeti
argumenta, sonant.
sentences.l: and garlands hang from the roofs, and everywhere lyres and pipe and singing - the happy proofs of a glad heart - sound.
sentences.i: Garlands hang from the roofs, and everywhere lyres, pipe and song ring out, the happy evidence of a glad heart.
sentences.n: "animi felicia laeti argumenta" stands in apposition to the three subjects, gathered into a single neuter plural; "argumenta" is a word from the law courts, the evidence produced for a case, and Ovid likes the legal term dropped into a domestic scene. Note the interlocking order (animi felicia laeti argumenta), adjectives split from their nouns and crossed over - normal in hexameter and rarely reproducible in English.

sentences.t:
Reseratis aurea valvis
atria tota patent,
sentences.l: The doors being unbarred, the golden halls lie wholly open,
sentences.i: With the doors thrown back, the golden halls stand open from end to end,
sentences.n: "Reseratis ... valvis" is an ablative absolute: a noun and participle in the ablative, self-contained, saying "with X done" where English wants a whole clause ("once the doors had been unbarred"). It is one of the commonest constructions in the poem and you will meet it again and again in this part - visa Medusa, te spectante, telo remisso, se prohibente and more.

sentences.t:
pulchroque instructa paratu
Cepheni proceres ineunt convivia regis.
sentences.l: and, furnished with beautiful appointments, the banquets of the Cephenian king the chieftains enter upon.
sentences.i: and the chieftains sit down to the banquet of the Cephenian king, laid out in splendid style.
sentences.n: "instructa" is neuter plural and belongs to "convivia", the banquet, not to the nobles who enter it, though four words separate participle from noun. The Cephenes are Cepheus' people, so the king is named by his subjects rather than by his own name - a habit of this poem, which will also name Perseus himself four different ways in this part - Abantiades, Agenorides, Danaeius heros, Acrisioniades - beside his own name.

sentences.t:
Postquam epulis functi generosi munere Bacchi
diffudere animos, cultusque genusque locorum
quaerit Abantiades:
sentences.l: After, the feast performed, they had unbent their spirits with the gift of noble Bacchus, the descendant of Abas asks the way of life and the character of the region:
sentences.i: When the feast was done and the gift of noble Bacchus had loosened their spirits, Perseus asks about the region's way of life and character.
sentences.n: "diffudere" is diffuderunt: the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere, which Ovid uses constantly for metre and speed. Recognise it as a perfect, not an infinitive - you will see tenuere, dixere, coiere and their like on nearly every page. "functi" from fungor takes the ablative "epulis". "Abantiades" is a patronymic, "descendant of Abas", meaning Perseus, whose great-grandfather Abas was king of Argos.

sentences.t:
quaerenti protinus unus
narrat Lyncides moresque animumque virorum
sentences.l: to him asking, at once one man, Lyncides, tells the customs and the temper of the men.
sentences.i: and to his question one of them, Lyncides, tells at once the manners and the temper of the people.
sentences.n: "quaerenti" is a bare dative participle standing for a whole clause, "to [the man] asking", i.e. in answer to his question; Latin does in one word what English needs a relative clause for, and you will meet the same trick at "Conanti" and "surgentibus" below. "Lyncides" means "descendant of Lynceus", which by blood is Perseus' own line, so its use here of one of Cepheus' courtiers is a long-standing difficulty: some editors read a dative, "one man tells the descendant of Lynceus".

sentences.t: Quae simul edocuit, “nunc, o fortissime,” dixit
sentences.l: As soon as he had taught these things through, “now, o bravest one,” he said,
sentences.i: The moment he had told it all out, “now, bravest of men,” he said,
sentences.n: "Quae" is a connecting relative: a relative pronoun opening a new sentence where English starts fresh with "and these things". "simul" alone here does the work of "simul ac", "as soon as", and "edocuit" is stronger than docuit - to teach a thing right through to the end. Magnus prints "Quae", making the subject-matter the link; some editions print "qui", making the speaker the link ("and he, as soon as he had explained").

sentences.t:
“fare, precor, Perseu, quanta virtute quibusque
artibus abstuleris crinita draconibus ora.”
sentences.l: “speak, I beg, Perseus, with how great courage and by what arts you carried off the head shaggy with serpents.”
sentences.i: “tell us, Perseus, I beg you, by what courage and by what arts you carried off that head with its mane of snakes.”
sentences.n: "fare" is the imperative of the defective deponent for, fari - a high, archaic verb kept for epic and prayer. "abstuleris" is subjunctive because "quanta ... quibus" open an indirect question, and Latin puts every indirect question into the subjunctive. "crinita draconibus ora" is literally "the face made-haired with serpents": "ora" is a poetic plural for one head, and "draconibus" is ablative of means with the participle.

sentences.t:
Narrat Agenorides gelido sub Atlante iacentem
esse locum solidae tutum munimine molis;
sentences.l: The descendant of Agenor tells that there lies, beneath chilly Atlas, a place safe by the defence of a solid mass;
sentences.i: Perseus tells them that beneath frozen Atlas lies a place fenced safe by a solid bulk of rock,
sentences.n: "narrat ... iacentem esse locum" is indirect statement - accusative subject plus infinitive - and it does not stop until line 787: every verb of the Gorgon story arrives as an infinitive (habitasse, cepisse, tetigisse, vidisse, adspexisse, eripuisse), so the whole adventure is held at one remove, reported rather than shown. "Agenorides", descendant of Agenor, is the second patronymic for Perseus in twenty lines. Atlas is here a mountain: Perseus had earlier turned him to stone with the Gorgon's head, so the place-name carries its own story.

sentences.t:
cuius in introitu geminas habitasse sorores
Phorcidas, unius partitas luminis usum.
sentences.l: that at its entrance dwelt the twin sisters, daughters of Phorcys, having divided between them the use of a single eye.
sentences.i: and that at its entrance lived the two Phorcid sisters, who shared the use of one eye between them.
sentences.n: The Phorcides, daughters of Phorcys, are the Graeae, grey from birth, with one eye between them which they hand from sister to sister. "partitas" is the perfect participle of the deponent partior and is active in sense, "having divided", not "having been divided" - deponent participles look passive and are not. "luminis" is "of the light" used for the organ that sees, a standard poetic transfer.

sentences.t:
Id se sollerti furtim, dum traditur, astu
supposita cepisse manu
sentences.l: That he, by clever cunning, stealthily, while it was being handed across, took it with a hand slipped underneath,
sentences.i: and that he took it by a clever trick, slipping his hand underneath while it was being passed across,
sentences.n: "Id" is the eye, picked up from "luminis" in the line before - Latin can carry a thing forward by a bare pronoun much longer than English can. "supposita ... manu" is an ablative of means with a participle hung on it, "with a hand put under" - not an ablative absolute, since the hand is the very instrument of "cepisse". "dum traditur" is present tense inside a past narrative: the historic present, which Ovid slides in and out of constantly to speed a moment up and hold it in front of the reader.

sentences.t:
perque abdita longe
deviaque et silvis horrentia saxa fragosis
Gorgoneas tetigisse domos,
sentences.l: and that through places far hidden and off the road, and rocks bristling with broken woodland, he reached the Gorgons' home,
sentences.i: and that through country hidden and far off the road, over crags bristling with tangled woods, he came to the Gorgons' house,
sentences.n: "abdita" and "devia" are neuter plural adjectives used as nouns, "hidden places", "places off the way" - Latin makes a noun out of an adjective far more readily than English, which has to supply the noun. "silvis ... fragosis" is ablative with "horrentia": the crags stand on end like hair that bristles, which is the same image the snake-haired head carries - "crinita draconibus ora" at 771 and the sleeping "colubrae" at 784.

sentences.t:
passimque per agros
perque vias vidisse hominum simulacra ferarumque
in silicem ex ipsis visa conversa Medusa.
sentences.l: and that everywhere through fields and along roads he had seen likenesses of men and of beasts, turned into flint out of their own selves, Medusa having been seen.
sentences.i: and that everywhere in the fields and along the roads he had seen the likenesses of men and beasts, changed out of their own flesh into stone at the sight of Medusa.
sentences.n: "visa ... Medusa" is an ablative absolute and the whole horror sits in it: not "because Medusa saw them" but "Medusa having been seen" - it is the victim's own look that kills him. "simulacra" is the word for a statue and for a ghost at once, so the field of stone figures is also a field of dead men. "ex ipsis" means out of their own selves: the stone is the man, not an image of him.

sentences.t:
Se tamen horrendae clipei, quem laeva gerebat,
aere repercusso formam adspexisse Medusae,
sentences.l: That he himself, however, in the beaten-back bronze of the shield which his left hand carried, had looked on the shape of dreadful Medusa,
sentences.i: that he himself, though, had looked at dreadful Medusa's shape in the beaten-back bronze of the shield his left arm carried,
sentences.n: "aere repercusso" is ablative of means: by the bronze that threw the image back, that is, in the reflection. The whole trick of the killing is packed into one participle. Watch how far "horrendae" is stretched from its noun "Medusae" - adjective at the end of one line, noun at the end of the next, with the shield's relative clause wedged between: the sentence keeps her at arm's length exactly as Perseus does. "laeva" is the left hand, with "manus" understood.

sentences.t:
dumque gravis somnus colubrasque ipsamque tenebat,
eripuisse caput collo;
sentences.l: and that, while heavy sleep held both the snakes and herself, he had torn the head from the neck;
sentences.i: and that, while deep sleep held her snakes and her together, he tore the head from the neck.
sentences.n: "colubrasque ipsamque" is the -que ... -que pairing, "both ... and", a Greek habit taken into Latin verse; it counts the snakes as sleepers separate from the woman. "collo" is a bare dative of separation, "from the neck", where prose would write ab plus the ablative - verse prefers the naked case.

sentences.t:
pennisque fugacem
Pegason et fratrem matris de sanguine natos
addidit et longi non falsa pericula cursus,
sentences.l: and he added Pegasus, swift in flight with his wings, and his brother, both born from their mother's blood, and the not-false dangers of his long journey,
sentences.i: and he added Pegasus, swift on his wings, and his brother, both born from their mother's blood, and the perils of his long flight, none of them invented,
sentences.n: "addidit" brings the sentence back out of indirect statement to a main verb, and the accusatives now hang from "he added [to his tale]" - Latin can make the contents of a story the direct object of a verb of adding. The brother is Chrysaor, sprung with Pegasus from Medusa's blood at the stroke that killed her; "matris" makes the beheaded woman a mother in the same breath. "non falsa" is litotes, asserting by denying the opposite, and it is a teller's wink at the exaggeration a story like this invites.

sentences.t:
quae freta, quas terras sub se vidisset ab alto
et quae iactatis tetigisset sidera pennis.
sentences.l: what seas, what lands he had seen beneath himself from on high, and what stars he had touched with tossing wings.
sentences.i: what seas and what lands he had seen below him from the height, and what stars he had brushed with beating wings.
sentences.n: Three more indirect questions (quae ... quas ... quae), so the verbs are subjunctive again: vidisset, tetigisset. "iactatis ... pennis" is ablative of means, the wings thrown about, the flapping itself. "sub se" holds the reader at Perseus' own altitude, looking down - the poem never leaves his eye.

sentences.t:
Ante exspectatum tacuit tamen. Excipit unus
ex numero procerum quaerens, cur sola sororum
gesserit alternis inmixtos crinibus angues.
sentences.l: Before the expected [moment] he fell silent, however. One from the number of the chieftains takes him up, asking why she alone of the sisters wore snakes mixed in among alternating hairs.
sentences.i: He fell silent, though, sooner than they expected. One of the chieftains takes him up, asking why she alone of the sisters wore snakes twined among her hair.
sentences.n: "Ante exspectatum" uses a past participle as a noun, "before the expected thing"; English cannot and needs a clause. "Excipit" is the technical word for taking up the talk where another leaves off, the polite move at a dinner table. "alternis ... crinibus" means strand alternating with snake; the question the guest asks - why her alone - is what produces the story of Medusa, and the answer will not be a comfortable one.

sentences.t:
Hospes ait: “Quoniam scitaris digna relatu,
accipe quaesiti causam.
sentences.l: The guest says: “Since you ask things worthy of the telling, receive the cause of what you asked.
sentences.i: The guest says: “Since what you ask is worth the telling, hear the reason behind your question.
sentences.n: "hospes" is one word for both guest and host, the two ends of a bond the Romans held sacred; Perseus is the guest here, and in the next book Cepheus will call on the gods of that same bond when Phineus breaks it at this very table. "digna relatu" uses the supine in -u after an adjective, a fixed idiom of the mirabile dictu type, "worthy in the telling". "scitaris" is deponent, "you inquire".

sentences.t:
Clarissima forma
multorumque fuit spes invidiosa procorum
illa:
sentences.l: Most famous in beauty, and the envied hope of many suitors, was she:
sentences.i: She was famous for her beauty, and the coveted hope of many suitors -
sentences.n: "forma" is ablative of respect, "in respect of her shape", the word covering face and figure together. "invidiosa" faces both ways at once: the hope that others envied, and the hope that drew ill-will down on her. Ovid holds "illa", the subject, back to the start of the next line, so everything is said about her before she is named at all.

sentences.t:
neque in tota conspectior ulla capillis
pars fuit. Inveni, qui se vidisse referret.
sentences.l: nor in the whole of her was any part more striking than the hair. I have found a man who would report that he had seen her.
sentences.i: and in all of her no part was more striking than her hair. I have met a man who said he had seen her himself.
sentences.n: "in tota" is "in the whole [woman]", the adjective standing alone for her. "conspectior" is a comparative of a participle-adjective, "more looked-at", with "capillis" as ablative of comparison. "Inveni, qui ... referret" is a relative clause of characteristic, subjunctive: not "I found the man who said" but "I found the sort of man who would say" - a witness exists. It is a strange quiet aside, a speaker vouching for hearsay in the middle of a monster story.

sentences.t:
Hanc pelagi rector templo vitiasse Minervae
dicitur.
sentences.l: Her the ruler of the sea is said to have violated in the temple of Minerva.
sentences.n: "vitiasse" (= vitiavisse) is the blunt Latin word for raping a woman - literally to spoil, to ruin her; it is the Latin's own hard euphemism and the English keeps its hardness rather than softening it. "pelagi rector" names Neptune by his office rather than his name, which is what the line does to him: no name, no blame. Follow the grammar - Medusa is the accusative object throughout, the god is the subject, and the punishment in the next line will land on her. The advisory at the head of this part covers it.

sentences.t:
Aversa est et castos aegide vultus
nata Iovis texit;
sentences.l: Jupiter's daughter turned herself away and covered her chaste face with the aegis;
sentences.n: "castos ... vultus" is the plain accusative object of the active "texit": Minerva covered her own chaste face with the aegis, "vultus" being the poetic plural for one face. "Aversa est" is passive in form and middle in sense, "she turned herself away". The aegis is Minerva's goatskin breastplate, and it will end this same story with the snakes she is about to make fixed to it.

sentences.t:
neve hoc inpune fuisset,
Gorgoneum crinem turpes mutavit in hydros.
sentences.l: and, so that this should not have gone unpunished, she changed the Gorgon's hair into foul water-snakes.
sentences.i: and so that it should not go unpunished, she changed the Gorgon's hair into vile snakes.
sentences.n: "neve ... fuisset" is a negative purpose clause with a pluperfect subjunctive, which puts the punishment in the goddess's mind as a thing already settled. Read the grammar for who is punished: the god is not in the sentence at all, and the verb falls on the woman he attacked. "turpes" carries Minerva's disgust, not the poem's - it is her word for what she has just made. Ovid states the whole thing without comment and lets it stand.

sentences.t:
Nunc quoque, ut attonitos formidine terreat hostes,
pectore in adverso, quos fecit, sustinet angues.”
sentences.l: Now too, so that she may terrify enemies struck senseless with dread, she carries on the front of her breast the snakes which she made.”
sentences.i: Even now, to strike her enemies senseless with terror, she carries on her breastplate the very snakes she made.”
sentences.n: "quoque" here is the adverb, "also, even now" - but watch the word: the same letters can be quo-que, "and with which", and only sense tells them apart. "quos fecit" is a relative clause cut into the middle of its own main clause, so that "the snakes" and "which she made" stand on either side of the verb. "attonitos ... terreat" states the result before the cause: struck senseless first, frightened second. The tale ends on the aegis it began with, and the poem runs on into Book V without a pause in the evening.

sentences.t:
Dumque ea Cephenum medio Danaeius heros
agmine commemorat, fremida regalia turba
atria complentur:
sentences.l: And while the hero, son of Danae, recounts these things in the middle of the Cephene throng, the royal halls are filled with a roaring crowd:
sentences.i: And while Danae's hero-son tells all this in the midst of the Cephene throng, the royal halls fill with a roaring crowd.
sentences.n: The book division falls in mid-scene: the feast, the guests and the story are the same ones Book IV left a line ago. "Danaeius heros" names Perseus by his mother, the third of the four epithets used for him in this part (Abantiades, Agenorides, Danaeius heros, and Acrisioniades to come) - the poem prefers a genealogy to a name, though it uses the plain "Perseus" too. "fremida ... turba" is ablative with "complentur"; fremidus, growling or roaring, is a rare word, and "medio ... agmine" is a bare ablative of place without a preposition, ordinary in verse.

sentences.t:
nec coniugialia festa
qui canat est clamor, sed qui fera nuntiet arma.
sentences.l: nor is it a shout such as would sing of a marriage feast, but such as would announce savage arms.
sentences.i: and the shout is not the kind that sings a wedding feast, but the kind that announces savage war.
sentences.n: "qui canat ... qui nuntiet" are two relative clauses of characteristic with the subjunctive: not "which sings" but "of a sort to sing". The noise is defined by what it is fit for, which lets Ovid turn a wedding into a war in one line without saying anything has happened yet. "fera arma" gives arms the adjective that belongs to wild beasts.

sentences.t:
Inque repentinos convivia versa tumultus
adsimilare freto possis, quod saeva quietum
ventorum rabies motis exasperat undis.
sentences.l: And the banquet turned into sudden uproar you could liken to a strait, quiet, which the savage madness of the winds roughens with the waves it has stirred.
sentences.i: You might liken the banquet, turned in a moment to uproar, to a quiet strait that the savage fury of the winds churns rough with the waves it raises.
sentences.n: "possis" is a potential subjunctive with an indefinite "you" - "one could" - and it is Ovid's way of compressing a full epic simile into a single sentence by inviting the reader to make the comparison instead of making it himself. "motis ... undis" is an ablative absolute again. "quietum" is held to the end of its line, four words away from "freto", so the sea is still calm when the line breaks and the winds - "ventorum rabies" - arrive in the next one.

sentences.t:
Primus in his Phineus, belli temerarius auctor,
fraxineam quatiens aeratae cuspidis hastam,
“en” ait, “en adsum praereptae coniugis ultor,
sentences.l: First among these Phineus, the reckless instigator of the war, shaking an ash spear with a bronze-shod point: “look,” he says, “look, I am here, the avenger of a wife snatched away,
sentences.i: First among them Phineus, the rash author of the war, brandishing an ash spear with a bronze-shod point: “here,” he says, “here I am, the avenger of a wife stolen from me,
sentences.n: Phineus is Cepheus' brother and Andromeda's uncle, to whom she had been promised: the marriage celebrated in the previous scene is the theft he claims to be avenging. "fraxineam ... hastam" names the shaft by its wood, the standard epic way of specifying a weapon. "coniugis" already calls her his wife - his word, and no wedding of his ever took place - and "praereptae" means snatched before he could take her.

sentences.t:
nec mihi te pennae, nec falsum versus in aurum
Iuppiter eripiet.”
sentences.l: and neither your wings nor Jupiter, turned into false gold, shall snatch you from me.”
sentences.i: and neither your wings nor Jupiter, who turned himself into a lie of gold, shall snatch you out of my hands.”
sentences.n: "mihi" is a dative of separation with eripiet, "snatch from me", the bare dative where English must say "from". "falsum versus in aurum": Jupiter came to Danae, shut up in her tower, as a shower of gold, and "falsum" makes the gold counterfeit because it was a god pretending - Phineus grants Perseus his divine father and sneers at him in the same phrase. "pennae" are the winged sandals.

sentences.t:
Conanti mittere Cepheus
“quid facis?” exclamat, “quae te, germane, furentem
mens agit in facinus?
sentences.l: To him attempting to throw, Cepheus cries out “what are you doing? What thought drives you, raving, brother, into the crime?
sentences.i: As he tries to throw, Cepheus cries out: “what are you doing? What thought drives you, brother, out of your senses and into this crime?
sentences.n: "Conanti" is the dative participle standing for a clause again, "to [him] as he was trying" - the same compression as "quaerenti" at IV.767. "germane" is the vocative for a brother by blood, and Cepheus puts the family tie first because his whole argument is built on it. "furentem" agrees with "te": "you in your madness", the state the crime is committed from.

sentences.t:
meritisne haec gratia tantis
redditur? hac vitam servatae dote rependis?
sentences.l: Is this the thanks that is returned for services so great? Do you repay the life of a woman saved with this dowry?
sentences.i: Is this the return made for services so great? Is this the dowry with which you pay back a life saved?
sentences.n: The particle -ne attached to "meritis" turns the sentence into a question, and the word order puts the services first so that the answering spear looks worse. "dote" picks up the dowry of IV.758, where the deed itself was the dowry: Phineus' answering gift is a weapon. "servatae" is a participle used as a noun, "of the woman saved", which Latin can do in one word and English cannot.

sentences.t: Quam tibi non Perseus, verum si quaeris, ademit,
sentences.l: And her it was not Perseus who took from you, if you want the truth,
sentences.i: And it was not Perseus who took her from you, if you want the truth,
sentences.n: "Quam" is a connecting relative opening a new sentence, "and her". "verum si quaeris" is a conversational idiom, "if it's the truth you're after", dropped into a formal rebuke. "tibi" is again the dative of separation with a verb of taking away.

sentences.t:
sed grave Nereidum numen, sed corniger Ammon,
sed quae visceribus veniebat belua ponti
exsaturanda meis.
sentences.l: but the heavy godhead of the Nereids, but horned Ammon, but the beast of the sea which was coming to be glutted on my own flesh.
sentences.i: but the crushing power of the Nereids, but horned Ammon, but the sea-beast that was coming to gorge itself on my own flesh.
sentences.n: Three "sed"s in a row (anaphora) move the blame off Perseus in three strokes. The story behind them: Andromeda's mother boasted against the Nereids, the oracle of Ammon - Jupiter in his Libyan form, with a ram's horns - ordered the girl chained to the rock, and the sea-beast came for her. "exsaturanda" is a gerundive of purpose, "to be glutted full". "visceribus ... meis" is a father counting his daughter as his own flesh and blood, not a metaphor he expects to be argued with.

sentences.t:
Illo tibi tempore rapta est,
quo peritura fuit:
sentences.l: At that time she was snatched from you, at which she was going to perish:
sentences.i: She was taken from you at the very moment when she was going to die -
sentences.n: "peritura fuit" is the future participle with a past tense of sum, a past future: the doom stood over her then and was certain. Cepheus takes Phineus' own charge of theft and dates it exactly - the theft happened at the moment the death sentence did, which is his answer to it.

sentences.t:
nisi si crudelis id ipsum
exigis, ut pereat, luctuque levabere nostro.
sentences.l: unless, cruel man, you are demanding this very thing, that she perish, and will be relieved by our grief.
sentences.i: unless - cruel as you are - that is exactly what you want, that she should die, and you mean to lighten your heart with our grief.
sentences.n: "nisi si" is a doubled "unless if", a colloquial reinforcement Latin allows and English will not carry twice. "levabere" is levaberis: the alternative second-singular passive ending in -re, very common in verse and easy to mistake for an infinitive. "luctu ... nostro" is ablative of means - the father's mourning is the medicine Phineus is accused of wanting.

sentences.t:
Scilicet haud satis est, quod te spectante revincta est
et nullam quod opem patruus sponsusve tulisti:
sentences.l: Of course it is not enough that she was bound fast with you looking on, and that you brought no help at all, either as her uncle or as her betrothed:
sentences.i: No doubt it is not enough that she was chained up while you watched, and that you brought no help, neither as her uncle nor as her promised husband.
sentences.n: "Scilicet" is heavy sarcasm here - "oh, naturally". "te spectante" is an ablative absolute and the whole charge sits inside it: he was there and watched. "patruus sponsusve" names his two claims on her, father's brother and promised husband, and he used neither. The two "quod" clauses are clauses of fact hanging from "satis est".

sentences.t:
insuper, a quoquam quod sit servata, dolebis
praemiaque eripies?
sentences.l: on top of that, will you grieve that she was saved by anyone at all, and snatch away the prize?
sentences.i: on top of that, will you resent her being saved by anyone at all, and snatch the prize away?
sentences.n: "a quoquam" is the sting: not "by Perseus" but "by anyone whatever", so the grievance is shown to be about the rescue rather than the rescuer. "sit servata" is subjunctive in a quod-clause giving the alleged ground of the grief. "praemia" is the same word IV.757 used for Andromeda herself, and in Phineus' hands it has become plunder.

sentences.t:
Quae si tibi magna videntur,
ex illis scopulis, ubi erant adfixa, petisses.
sentences.l: And if these things seem great to you, you should have sought them from those rocks where they were fastened.
sentences.i: And if the prize seems so great to you, you should have gone to fetch it from the rocks where it was chained.
sentences.n: "Quae" is a connecting relative again, picking up "praemia". "petisses" (= petivisses) is a pluperfect subjunctive standing alone as a reproach for what was not done: "you ought to have gone". "adfixa" keeps the neuter plural of praemia, so grammatically it is the prize that was nailed to the rock - Cepheus holds Phineus' own cold word up against the picture of his chained daughter.

sentences.t:
Nunc sine, qui petiit, per quem haec non orba senectus,
ferre quod et meritis et voce est pactus, eumque
non tibi, sed certae praelatum intellege morti!”
sentences.l: Now let the man who did go for her, through whom this old age is not childless, carry off what he bargained for both by his deserts and by the spoken word; and understand that he was preferred not to you, but to certain death!”
sentences.i: Now let the man who did go for her - the man through whom my old age is not childless - carry off what he earned by his deeds and by my given word; and understand that he was chosen not over you, but over certain death.”
sentences.n: "sine" is the imperative of sino, "allow", and it governs the infinitive "ferre" four words later, with two relative clauses wedged in between - hold the "let" open until the infinitive arrives. "haec ... senectus", "this old age", is the old man pointing at himself instead of saying "I"; "orba" is the word for a parent robbed of a child. "praelatum ... morti" is the dative with prae-fero, "preferred to": Cepheus turns the jealousy inside out, since the rival Perseus beat was not a suitor but the sea.

sentences.t:
Ille nihil contra: sed et hunc et Persea vultu
alterno spectans petat hunc ignorat, an illum,
sentences.l: He [says] nothing in answer: but looking at both this man and Perseus with alternating face, he does not know whether to go for this one or that,
sentences.i: He answers nothing: looking from one to the other, from Cepheus to Perseus and back, he cannot tell which of them to strike.
sentences.n: "nihil contra" has no verb at all - the ellipse of "said" is ordinary Latin, and here it is dramatic: Phineus has no answer to make. "petat ... an" is a deliberative subjunctive inside an indirect question, "whether he should attack". "vultu alterno" is what makes the hesitation visible: his face goes back and forth between the two men.

sentences.t:
cunctatusque brevi contortam viribus hastam,
quantas ira dabat, nequiquam in Persea misit.
sentences.l: and having hesitated a short while, he sent the spear, whirled with such strength as anger gave, in vain at Perseus.
sentences.i: and after a brief hesitation he hurled the spear, wound up with all the strength his anger gave, at Perseus - and in vain.
sentences.n: "brevi" is a neuter ablative doing an adverb's work, "in a short [time]". "quantas ira dabat" is a clause of amount slipped in between the spear and the verb that throws it, so the strength is measured by the rage. "nequiquam" comes before the throw is finished: the reader is told it fails before it lands, which is how the poem keeps Perseus untouchable.

sentences.t:
Ut stetit illa toro, stratis tunc denique Perseus
exsiluit;
sentences.l: When it stood fast in the couch, then at last Perseus leapt up from the cushions;
sentences.i: When it stuck fast in the couch, only then did Perseus spring up from the cushions;
sentences.n: "Ut" with the perfect indicative means "when", not "in order that" - the mood and tense are what tell the two uses apart. "stetit" of a weapon means it landed and held, the spear standing upright in the furniture. "tunc denique" is the point of the scene: the wedding guests are still reclining at table, and Perseus does not get up until the spear is in the couch.

sentences.t:
teloque ferox inimica remisso
pectora rupisset, nisi post altaria Phineus
isset: et (indignum!) scelerato profuit ara.
sentences.l: and, fierce, with the weapon sent back, he would have burst the hostile breast, had Phineus not gone behind the altars: and - outrageous! - the altar did a criminal good.
sentences.i: and fierce with the spear sent back at its owner he would have burst his enemy's breast, had Phineus not got behind the altars: and - the shame of it - the altar served a criminal.
sentences.n: A past contrary-to-fact condition: "rupisset ... nisi ... isset", both pluperfect subjunctive, saying what would have happened and did not. "telo remisso" is an ablative absolute, and it is the same spear returned to the man who threw it. "(indignum!)" is an exclamatory accusative, the narrator breaking in for a single word - Ovid's outrage, not Cepheus'. The altars stand in the hall where the feast is being held, and sanctuary, being a rule, protects the guilty as readily as the innocent.

sentences.t: Fronte tamen Rhoeti non inrita cuspis adhaesit.
sentences.l: In the forehead of Rhoetus, however, the point stuck, not ineffectual.
sentences.i: Still, the point found its mark and lodged in Rhoetus' forehead.
sentences.n: "non inrita" is litotes once more, "not without effect" for "deadly"; Ovid keeps the understatement for the killings, where saying less does more. "Fronte" is a bare ablative of place. Rhoetus is named in order to be killed: from here the battle fills with men who get a name, a country and a wound in a single line each, which is how epic catalogues of the dead work.

sentences.t:
Qui postquam cecidit ferrumque ex osse revulsum est,
calcitrat et positas adspergit sanguine mensas.
sentences.l: And he, after he fell and the iron was wrenched out of the bone, kicks and spatters the laid tables with blood.
sentences.n: "Qui" opens the sentence as a connecting relative, "and he". Watch the tenses change hands: the perfects (cecidit, revulsum est) report what is over, and then the presents (calcitrat, adspergit) put the dying in front of the reader - the historic present used for exactly the moment Ovid wants held. "positas ... mensas" are tables "placed", that is, set for the feast: the wedding furniture is what the blood lands on.

sentences.t:
Tum vero indomitas ardescit vulgus in iras,
telaque coniciunt, et sunt, qui Cephea dicunt
cum genero debere mori.
sentences.l: Then indeed the crowd blazes up into ungovernable rages, and they hurl weapons, and there are men who say that Cepheus ought to die along with his son-in-law.
sentences.i: Then the crowd truly blazes into ungovernable fury, and they hurl their weapons, and there are men who say Cepheus should die along with his son-in-law.
sentences.n: "vulgus" is neuter singular but takes a plural verb two words later ("coniciunt") - a collective noun pulling the grammar over to its sense, which here turns a mass into many separate hands. "sunt qui ... dicunt" with the indicative asserts that such men actually exist; the subjunctive would have kept them a mere type. "in iras" is a poetic plural, rages rather than rage, for a feeling spread over a crowd.

sentences.t:
Sed limine tecti
exierat Cepheus, testatus iusque fidemque
hospitiique deos, ea se prohibente moveri.
sentences.l: But Cepheus had gone out from the threshold of the house, having called to witness right and good faith and the gods of hospitality, that these things were being set in motion with him forbidding it.
sentences.i: But Cepheus had gone out over the threshold, calling right and good faith and the gods of guest-friendship to witness that this was being done against his forbidding.
sentences.n: "se prohibente" is an ablative absolute that lets him disclaim the entire riot in two words, "with him forbidding". "testatus" is from the deponent testor and is active in sense. "hospitii ... deos": guest-friendship stands under divine protection, and Phineus, attacking his host's guest at his host's table, is breaking the very bond that IV.793 named with the word "hospes". Cepheus' pluperfect ("exierat") quietly removes him before the killing starts.

sentences.t:
Bellica Pallas adest et protegit aegide fratrem
datque animos.
sentences.l: Warlike Pallas is at hand, and protects her brother with the aegis, and gives him courage.
sentences.n: "fratrem" is doing the naming: Perseus is Jupiter's son, so Minerva is his half-sister, and the Latin gives the relationship where English would give the name. "Bellica Pallas" is the same "bellica virgo" addressed at the turf altars at IV.754, and the aegis is the one she covered her face with at IV.799 - the goddess arrives on the battlefield carrying the object her own story in this part is made of.

sentences.t:
Erat Indus Athis, quem flumine Gange
edita Limnaee vitreis peperisse sub undis
creditur,
sentences.l: There was an Indian, Athis, whom Limnaee, brought forth from the river Ganges, is believed to have borne beneath the glassy waves,
sentences.i: There was an Indian, Athis, whom Limnaee, daughter of the river Ganges, is believed to have borne beneath the glassy waters,
sentences.n: "Erat" opening a sentence is the storyteller's "there was once a man", and in a battle scene it always means the man is about to be killed; Ovid starts each of these vignettes the same way. "creditur" is used personally, with the nominative "Limnaee" as its subject and "peperisse" as the infinitive - Latin says "Limnaee is believed to have borne him" where English says "it is believed that ..."; either way the divine parentage is kept at one remove, what people believe rather than what the poem asserts. "edita" from edo is "brought forth", with "flumine Gange" as ablative of origin.

sentences.t:
egregius forma, quam divite cultu
augebat, bis adhuc octonis integer annis,
sentences.l: outstanding in beauty, which he increased with rich adornment, still untouched at twice eight years,
sentences.i: outstanding in beauty, which he set off with rich dress, still unspoiled at twice eight years old,
sentences.n: "bis ... octonis ... annis" is sixteen said as a sum, the distributive octoni doubled; verse counts in figures like this because plain numerals will not fit a hexameter. "integer" is "whole, untouched, unmarked" - and the word is answered eight lines later by the broken bones of his face at V.58. "forma" is ablative of respect again.

sentences.t:
indutus chlamydem Tyriam, quam limbus obibat
aureus;
sentences.l: clothed as to a Tyrian cloak, which a golden border ran round;
sentences.i: wearing a Tyrian cloak with a golden border running round it;
sentences.n: "indutus chlamydem" is the Greek accusative of respect after a passive participle - literally "clothed as to a cloak", not "the cloak was put on him"; English has only "wearing". Tyrian means dyed with the purple of Tyre, the most expensive colour in the ancient world: Ovid is spending money on a boy he is about to kill.

sentences.t:
ornabant aurata monilia collum
et madidos murra curvum crinale capillos.
sentences.l: gilded necklaces adorned his neck, and a curved hair-clasp his hair, drenched with myrrh.
sentences.i: gilded chains adorned his neck, and a curved clasp his hair, soaked with myrrh.
sentences.n: One verb ("ornabant") serves both halves and the second half does without it - zeugma again, and it lets the line run at twice the speed. "madidos murra ... capillos" wraps participle and noun round the whole phrase, with "murra" as ablative of means. Perfumed and jewelled hair marks an eastern prince, and it is the head that will be struck.

sentences.t:
Ille quidem iaculo quamvis distantia misso
figere doctus erat, sed tendere doctior arcus.
sentences.l: He indeed had been taught to pierce things however far off with a hurled javelin, but was better taught to bend the bow.
sentences.i: He had been trained to hit things at any distance with a thrown javelin, but trained better still at bending the bow.
sentences.n: "quamvis distantia" is a participle used as a neuter plural noun, "however-far-off things"; Latin builds nouns out of participles freely and English must supply a noun. "doctus ... doctior" repeats the word rather than replacing it, so the second skill grows out of the first. The bow is not decoration: his friend will take up this very bow eight lines later.

sentences.t:
Tunc quoque lenta manu flectentem cornua Perseus
stipite, qui media positus fumabat in ara,
perculit et fractis confudit in ossibus ora.
sentences.l: Then too, as he was bending the pliant horns with his hand, Perseus struck him with a brand which lay smoking on the middle altar, and mixed his face together amid the broken bones.
sentences.i: Then too, while he was bending the pliant bow-tips with his hand, Perseus struck him with a log that lay smoking on the middle altar, and crushed his face into the shattered bone.
sentences.n: "quoque" is again the adverb, "then too", not "and with which" - the trap is worth a second look every time. "cornua" are the horn tips of the bow, the weapon named by its material. The "middle altar" is Jupiter's, the middle one of the three built at IV.755, so the wedding's own furniture becomes the weapon. "confudit ... ora" is exact and ugly: to pour together, to mix into one mass, so that face and bone can no longer be told apart.

sentences.t:
Hunc ubi laudatos iactantem in sanguine vultus
Assyrius vidit Lycabas, iunctissimus illi
et comes et veri non dissimulator amoris,
sentences.l: When Assyrian Lycabas saw him tossing his praised face in his blood - Lycabas, most closely joined to him, both his companion and no concealer of a true love -
sentences.i: When Assyrian Lycabas saw him tossing that admired face in the blood - Lycabas, bound closest to him, his companion, and no man to hide a love that was real -
sentences.n: "laudatos ... vultus" means the face that has just been praised, and the participle drags the whole preceding description of the boy into the wreck of it. "non dissimulator" is litotes doing serious work: the Latin says plainly that the two men were lovers and that Lycabas made no secret of it. "iunctissimus" is the superlative of a participle, "most joined", and the same root returns at line 73 in "iunctae ... mortis".

sentences.t:
postquam exhalantem sub acerbo vulnere vitam
deploravit Athin, quos ille tetenderat arcus
arripit
sentences.l: after he had wept aloud for Athis breathing out his life under the bitter wound, he snatches up the bow which that one had bent
sentences.i: after weeping aloud over Athis as he breathed his life out under that bitter wound, he snatches up the bow Athis had bent,
sentences.n: "exhalantem ... vitam" agrees with Athin: he is breathing his life out, and Ovid keeps the object as concrete as breath. "acerbo" means unripe as much as bitter - it is the standing word for a death that comes too early, and Athis is sixteen. "quos ... arcus" draws the antecedent inside its own relative clause - "which bow he had bent" - a turn English cannot copy, and the plural "arcus" is a poetic plural for one bow.

sentences.t:
et “mecum tibi sint certamina” dixit:
“nec longum pueri fato laetabere, quo plus
invidiae, quam laudis habes.”
sentences.l: and said “let your contests be with me: and you will not rejoice long in a boy's death, from which you get more of ill-will than of praise.”
sentences.i: and said: “let your fight be with me - and you will not rejoice long in a boy's death, which earns you more hatred than praise.”
sentences.n: "mecum tibi sint certamina" is a jussive subjunctive with a dative of the person concerned: "let there be contests for you with me", i.e. fight me instead. "laetabere" is laetaberis, the -re ending again, and laetor takes the ablative "fato". "quo" is that ablative picked up by a relative, "by which death". Lycabas argues in the standard currency of epic - reputation - which is the only weapon he has left.

sentences.t:
Haec omnia nondum
dixerat, emicuit nervo penetrabile telum
vitatumque tamen sinuosa veste pependit.
sentences.l: He had not yet said all this - the piercing shaft flashed out from the string, and, dodged even so, hung in the folded garment.
sentences.i: He had not finished saying all this when the piercing shaft flashed from the string - dodged, even so, and left hanging in the folds of the cloak.
sentences.n: The two clauses are set side by side with no "when" between them at all: parataxis, where Latin leaves out the join and lets the speed carry the sense. "penetrabile" is active in meaning, "able to pierce", though the -bilis ending usually looks passive in English; verse adjectives in -bilis go either way. "vitatum ... pependit" describes the near miss from the arrow's side: avoided, and caught in the cloth all the same.

sentences.t:
Vertit in hunc harpen spectatam caede Medusae
Acrisioniades adigitque in pectus:
sentences.l: The descendant of Acrisius turns against him the hooked sword proved in the slaughter of Medusa, and drives it into his breast:
sentences.i: Acrisius' descendant turns on him the hooked sword proved in Medusa's killing, and drives it into his chest.
sentences.n: "harpe" is a Greek word kept in Greek shape (accusative harpen): the hooked sickle-sword Perseus beheaded Medusa with, so the weapon is named by its history rather than its make. "spectatam" means tested and proved by trial, a word used of assayed metal and of tried men. "Acrisioniades" is the third patronymic for Perseus in this part - after Abantiades and Agenorides, "Danaeius heros" being drawn from his mother - and the coldest of them: Acrisius is the grandfather who shut Danae in the tower.

sentences.t:
at ille
iam moriens, oculis sub nocte natantibus atra
circumspexit Athin seque acclinavit ad illum
et tulit ad manes iunctae solacia mortis.
sentences.l: but he, already dying, with eyes swimming beneath a black night, looked round for Athis and leaned himself towards him, and carried down to the shades the consolation of a joined death.
sentences.i: but he, already dying, his eyes swimming under a black night, looked round for Athis, leaned himself against him, and carried down to the shades the comfort of a death shared.
sentences.n: "oculis ... natantibus" is an ablative absolute, the eyes swimming as the dark closes over them - drowning used as the image for the moment of death. "sub nocte ... atra" wraps the adjective round the participle so the darkness shuts on the eyes in the word order too. "iunctae ... mortis" answers the "iunctissimus" of line 60: the joining held, and it is the only comfort the poem gives him. The "manes" are the spirits of the dead and, by extension, the place they go.

sentences.t:
Ecce Syenites, genitus Metione, Phorbas
et Libys Amphimedon, avidi committere pugnam,
sanguine, quo late tellus madefacta tepebat,
conciderant lapsi:
sentences.l: Look - Phorbas of Syene, begotten of Metion, and Libyan Amphimedon, greedy to join the fight, had slipped and fallen in the blood with which the earth, soaked far and wide, was lying warm:
sentences.i: Then Phorbas of Syene, Metion's son, and Amphimedon the Libyan, eager to join the fight, slipped and went down in the blood that had soaked the ground far and wide and lay warm on it.
sentences.n: "Ecce" hands the scene straight to the reader as though it were visible - the narrator's pointing finger, and a regular signal in these battle sequences that a new pair of victims has arrived. "avidi committere" is an adjective governing an infinitive, a Greek-flavoured licence prose would not allow (prose wants a gerund). "tepebat" is "was warm": the ground has been given the temperature of a body. Syene is Aswan on the Nile, so the dead are being drawn from the whole Egyptian and Libyan south.

sentences.t:
surgentibus obstitit ensis,
alterius costis, iugulo Phorbantis adactus.
sentences.l: as they were rising the sword stood in the way, driven into the ribs of the one, into the throat of Phorbas.
sentences.i: as they rose, the sword was there to meet them - driven into the ribs of the one, into the throat of Phorbas.
sentences.n: "surgentibus" is another bare dative participle carrying a whole clause, "for them as they were getting up" - the third of these in this part. "obstitit" understates savagely: the sword merely "got in their way". One participle, "adactus", governs both datives (costis, iugulo), so two men are killed inside a single piece of grammar.

sentences.t:
At non Actoriden Erytum, cui lata bipennis
telum erat, hamato Perseus petit ense,
sentences.l: But Erytus, son of Actor, whose weapon was a broad double axe, Perseus does not go for with the hooked sword,
sentences.i: But Perseus does not attack Erytus, son of Actor - whose weapon was a broad double axe - with the hooked sword,
sentences.n: "cui ... telum erat" is the dative of possession, "to whom there was a weapon" - the ordinary Latin way of saying "he had one", and worth recognising because the owner appears in the dative rather than the nominative. "bipennis" is the two-winged, double-headed axe, and naming it marks Erytus as a heavy fighter, which is why the sword will not serve. "non" stands at the head of the sentence, so the reader waits a line and a half to find out what Perseus uses instead.

sentences.t:
sed altis
exstantem signis multaeque in pondere massae
ingentem manibus tollit cratera duabus
infligitque viro;
sentences.l: but a mixing-bowl standing out with high reliefs and huge in the weight of its great mass he lifts with both hands and dashes against the man;
sentences.i: but lifts in both hands a mixing-bowl embossed with high reliefs, huge in the sheer weight of its metal, and dashes it down on the man;
sentences.n: "cratera" is a Greek accusative: the great bowl in which wine and water were mixed at a feast - once again the banquet's own furniture becomes the weapon, as the altar-brand did at line 57. "exstantem signis" means standing out with figures, i.e. worked in relief (Magnus keeps the spelling exst-). Two accusative modifiers, "exstantem" and "ingentem", pile up before their noun arrives, so the reader feels the weight of the thing for two and a half lines before learning what it is.

sentences.t:
rutilum vomit ille cruorem
et resupinus humum moribundo vertice pulsat.
sentences.l: he vomits red gore and, laid on his back, beats the ground with his dying head.
sentences.i: he vomits red blood and, flat on his back, beats the ground with his dying head.
sentences.n: "cruor" is spilt blood, as against "sanguis", the blood inside a living body; Latin keeps the two apart and this poem keeps the distinction. "moribundo vertice" gives the adjective of the whole man to the crown of his head, so the part dies on its own. "resupinus" is an adjective doing an adverb's work, "on his back", which Latin much prefers to an adverb.

sentences.t:
Inde Semiramio Polydegmona sanguine cretum
Caucasiumque Abarin Sperchionidenque Lycetum
intonsumque comas Helicen Phlegyanque Clytumque
sternit et exstructos morientum calcat acervos.
sentences.l: Next Polydegmon, sprung from Semiramis' blood, and Caucasian Abaris and Lycetus son of Sperchios, and Helix unshorn as to his hair, and Phlegyas and Clytus he lays low, and treads on the heaped-up piles of the dying.
sentences.i: Next he lays low Polydegmon, sprung from Semiramis' blood, Abaris of the Caucasus, Lycetus son of Sperchios, Helix with his hair unshorn, Phlegyas and Clytus - and treads the heaped piles of the dying.
sentences.n: Six names in three lines, all accusatives waiting on one verb ("sternit") at the head of the fourth: the catalogue of the slain is a set piece of epic, and holding the verb to the end makes the six killings a single continuous act. "intonsum ... comas" is the Greek accusative of respect once more, "unshorn as to his hair". Semiramis is the legendary queen of Babylon and Sperchios a Greek river-god - the dead are gathered from everywhere. "morientum" (= morientium) is present: they are still dying while he walks over them.

sentences.t:
Nec Phineus ausus concurrere comminus hosti,
intorquet iaculum:
sentences.l: And Phineus, not having dared to run against his enemy hand to hand, hurls a javelin:
sentences.n: "ausus" is the perfect participle of a semi-deponent (audeo, ausus sum) and is active in sense: "having dared", never "having been dared". "comminus", from manus, means hand to hand, and it is the standard measure of courage in a battle scene; the poem denies it to Phineus in the same breath in which it gives him a throw. "hosti" is dative with "concurrere", the compound verb taking the case its prefix wants.

sentences.t:
quod detulit error in Idan,
expertem frustra belli et neutra arma secutum.
sentences.l: and a straying carried it aside into Idas, who had no part in the war, in vain, and had followed neither side's arms.
sentences.i: and a stray flight carried it into Idas, who had kept out of the war - to no purpose - and had followed neither side's arms.
sentences.n: "error" is not a mistake here but a wandering, the flight going astray; Latin abstract nouns often name the event rather than the quality. "frustra" belongs with "expertem": his neutrality did him no good, and the adverb is set where it spoils the word in front of it. "neutra arma" - neither set of arms - is the definition of the neutral man, whom the battle kills anyway.

sentences.l: He, looking at pitiless Phineus with grim eyes, says “since I am being dragged into taking sides, receive, Phineus, the enemy you have made, and pay wound for wound with this one”;
sentences.i: He, eyeing pitiless Phineus with a grim look, says: “since I am dragged into taking sides, then take, Phineus, the enemy you have made, and settle this wound with a wound”;
sentences.n: "in partes ... abstrahor" uses the political word for factions, and the passive puts the choice outside him: he did not take a side, he was hauled onto one. "accipe ... quem fecisti hostem" swallows the antecedent into its own relative clause, so "the enemy" arrives inside the clause that made him one. "pensa ... vulnus" is from weighing out money: settle the account, wound weighed against wound.

sentences.t:
iamque remissurus tractum de vulnere telum
sanguine defectos cecidit conlapsus in artus.
sentences.l: and already about to send back the shaft drawn out of the wound, he fell, collapsing into limbs failed by his blood.
sentences.i: and, on the point of sending back the shaft he had drawn from the wound, he fell, collapsing into limbs his blood had already failed.
sentences.n: "remissurus" is the future participle used for what a man is about to do and does not do, which is the shape of this whole death. "sanguine defectos ... artus" is an ablative of cause: he falls into his own body as though into something else that will not hold him. Magnus prints "de vulnere", drawn from the wound; some editions print "de corpore", drawn from the body. The sequence ends mid-line, and the fighting goes straight on.
